newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian minister denies calling Tietmeyer "pig".
newsitem.headline: Austrian minister denies calling Tietmeyer "pig".

text.p: Austrian Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel on Monday denied media reports he called German Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer a "real pig" and brushed aside opposition calls for his resignation.

The German weekly magazine Focus alleged that Schuessel, who is also Austrian vice chancellor and leader of the conservative People's Party, made the remarks at a press breakfast during the European Union's June 16-17 summit in Amsterdam.
"This is a malicious misrepresentation. Such words do not belong to my vocabulary," Schuessel told Austrian state radio ORF.

Vienna daily Der Standard said the alleged outburst was triggered by a row between German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and the Bundesbank over the Bonn government's plans to revalue the central bank's gold reserves. Schuessel wanted to express solidarity with Waigel, Der Standard wrote.
Schuessel insisted he had not attended any press breakfast in Amsterdam.

He slammed down the telephone receiver when pressed on whether he had attacked Tietmeyer during another informal chat with journalists. ORF said two of its journalists had witnessed such a conversation.
Before aborting the radio interview, Schuessel was at pains to praise Tietmeyer and his efforts to ensure Europe's planned single currency got off to a timely start.
"Tietmeyer is an extraordinarily wise man with a great deal of foresight," said Schuessel, whose party rules in coalition with Chancellor Viktor Klima's Social Democrats.

He accused the German press of seeking revenge for his insistence that Austria should become part of the EU's border-free Schengen area. Austria, which lies at the bloc's eastern extremity, is due to join Schengen later this year despite German doubts over the security of its outer borders.
"This is clearly a case of sour grapes," Schuessel said.
Opposition parties were dissatisfied with the foreign minister's response and wasted no time in calling for his resignation if the allegations were true.
"(Schuessel) should not need to be told what to do if that is the case," said Peter Westenthaler, spokesman for the far-right Freedom Party.
He recommended a crash course at a finishing school for the vice chancellor, and warned the alleged incident threatened to do untold damage to Austria's image abroad.
